---
title: "Training on multiple devices"
---

![Forms of parallelism, from @raschka2023sometechniquestomakeyourpytorchmodel](images/forms_of_parallelism.png)

The installed API supports data parallelism: workers process different parts
of a global minibatch and average gradients before an optimizer update. Model
parallelism and multi-node launching are not supplied by this interface.

## Configure devices

After the [CUDA setup](../basics/installing_metis.qmd#optional-cuda-setup):

```bash
uv run metis train training.device=cuda training.num_devices=4 training.batch_size=128
```

`batch_size` is global and must divide evenly by `num_devices`; here each worker
processes 32 realizations. CUDA workers use NCCL and contiguous devices starting
at the selected CUDA index. Restrict visible GPUs when necessary:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 uv run metis train training.device=cuda training.num_devices=2 training.batch_size=128
```

CPU workers use Gloo:

```bash
uv run metis train training.device=cpu training.num_devices=2 training.batch_size=128
```

This is useful for correctness checks; multiprocessing overhead can make small
CPU jobs slower. One device remains the default. Device minibatching does not
make the simulation bank out of core: it must still fit in host memory.

The Python equivalent is `TrainingConfig(device="cuda", num_devices=4,
batch_size=128)`. Launch multiprocessing scripts under
`if __name__ == "__main__":`; use the installed CLI for a straightforward
notebook-to-terminal transition. Checkpoint resume requires the same topology.

## Troubleshooting

- Check visible GPU count and PyTorch CUDA availability before selecting CUDA.
- Check global batch-size divisibility.
- Use `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` to investigate CUDA communication failures.
- Establish a successful one-device run before diagnosing distributed behavior.

A passing CPU distributed test does not validate a CUDA driver/NCCL stack.
